meta.regime: Monday opened and settled the argument this page made on Sunday, by confirming half of it and refuting the other half. Oil did exactly what the re-escalation thesis said: Brent +2.64% to 107.074 and WTI +1.85% to 94.119. Everything that was supposed to come with it did the opposite. Gold fell 2.09% to 4195.62, silver 3.50% to 62.009, the franc weakened with USD/CHF up to 0.82972, and European equities rose - the DAX +0.30% to 25484, the Euro Stoxx 50 +0.38% to 6327, and the Euro Stoxx Banks index +1.38%. The US 10-year rose 4.4bp to 5.2090. Read those together and the regime has a name: this is an energy-inflation regime, not a risk-off regime. Higher crude feeds inflation, inflation feeds central banks, central banks feed yields, and rising nominal and real yields are a tax on havens rather than a call on them. The mechanism is visible in the reason the market gave for not panicking - Trump said he expects negotiations to resume this week, and Araghchi confirmed the rejection had still not been delivered through mediators. A delayed reopening is bullish crude and bullish rates. It is not a war premium.

dailyRead: Yesterday this page made a single call and staked six currency scores on it: Trump had rejected Iran's seven-day Hormuz roadmap on Saturday after the close, therefore the de-escalation trade was dead, therefore oil rallies, the franc bids, gold and silver bid, and European equities fall. Monday opened and graded that call. The oil half was right and the haven half was wrong, and the wrongness is more informative than the rightness, so start there. Brent is 107.074, up 2.64% on the day and 18.33% on the month; WTI is 94.119, up 1.85%. That is the re-escalation premium arriving on schedule. But gold fell 2.09% to 4195.62, silver fell 3.50% to 62.009, the franc weakened with USD/CHF up 0.18% to 0.82972, and the DAX and the Euro Stoxx 50 both rose, +0.30% to 25484 and +0.38% to 6327, with the Euro Stoxx Banks index up 1.38% - the strongest sector move on the board. A market that is frightened does not buy banks and sell gold. So what did the tape actually price? Two things, and both are verifiable. First, the diplomatic channel is not closed. Trump said Tehran had overplayed its hand and that he expects negotiations to resume this week, and as of Saturday Araghchi said the rejection had still not been communicated to Iran officially through mediators, while keeping diplomacy explicitly on the table even as he said Iran is prepared to resume fighting. He also claimed the US ambassador has not read the proposal. Iran's terms are unchanged: lift the naval blockade, waive sanctions on oil sales, and a ceasefire covering the wider region including Lebanon, in exchange for reopening the strait and restarting nuclear talks. A market told that a deal is delayed rather than dead buys the barrel and leaves the haven alone. Second, and this is the bigger driver, yields rose. The US 10-year is 5.2090, up 4.4bp, with the real yield near 2.84%, and the dollar firmed with DXY at 101.119. Gold at 4196 against a 5.2% ten-year is a documented pairing rather than an interpretation, and it is why the metals lost on a day they were supposed to win: no haven bid arrived and the carry got worse. Put those together and the week has a frame. This is an energy-inflation regime. Expensive crude is not a risk event here, it is an inflation event, and it transmits to FX through central banks rather than through fear. That reframing is what moves the board today, and it moves it in a specific direction: own the currencies whose central banks are being pushed to hike by energy, and sell the ones that cannot respond. The single biggest change is Canadian, and it is a fact this page did not have yesterday. Bond markets now put the odds of a 25bp Bank of Canada hike on October 28 at 68% against 32% for a hold. That is not a forecast, it is pricing, and it converts Governor Macklem's conditional into an active path. At the September 2 decision - the seventh consecutive hold at 2.25% - Macklem said the global energy shock remains the biggest tailwind to higher prices and that inflationary risks had become sharper since July, with oil persistently high and no end in sight to the conflict. Brent up 18.33% on the month is that condition, met. The domestic picture supports it more than it did: August retail sales rebounded 1.3% m/m after -0.7%, and Q2 GDP came in at 0.8% q/q and 1.1% y/y from 0.1%. What still caps CAD is the labour market and the surveys - August employment -41.7k after +75.1k, and services and composite PMIs at 46.8 and 47.8, still the only contracting PMIs on this board. So CAD goes from 0 to +1, and the practical consequence is that USD/CAD comes off LONG to RANGE: a 175bp rate gap is real, but when the Fed is 70% priced for October and the BoC is 68% priced for the same day, the gap stops widening, and the barrel now works against the long rather than for it. Monthly GDP tomorrow at 12:30Z, forecast 0.1% against 0.3%, is the test. The second change is Swiss and it is a two-notch downgrade, from 0 straight to -2, so it needs the specific reason stated. Yesterday the franc was upgraded on the argument that a war being re-escalated to a schedule is exactly when the franc bids. It was given the cleanest possible test - an escalation headline over a weekend, with crude up 2.64% on the Monday - and it did not bid. USD/CHF rose to 0.82972, up 1.04% on the week and 2.64% on the month, and gold falling 2.09% on the same session says the absence of haven demand is general rather than a franc quirk. Strip the haven leg out and what is left is the weakest structural position on this board, now verified from the SNB's own September 24 assessment: the policy rate is 0.00% for the fifth consecutive meeting, the conditional inflation forecast is 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for each of 2027 and 2028, and the Bank has returned to its standard wording that it is willing to be active in the FX market as necessary - which reads as a standing bid to sell francs, not buy them. Schlegel has ruled out enthusiasm for negative rates by citing their undesirable side effects, so 0.00% is the floor and also the ceiling of ambition. The Swiss 10-year is 0.6490, a 456bp disadvantage to the US. Swiss CPI on Thursday at 06:30Z is forecast at 0.0% m/m against 0.4%. A zero-rate currency with a flat CPI forecast, in a month when six of the other seven central banks are hiking or being pushed to, is a -2, and it makes the CHF crosses the cleanest longs on the page. The third change is Australian and it is a downgrade, from +3 to +2, which needs stating plainly because this page has been the loudest bull on AUD for a week. The RBA still hikes tomorrow at 04:30Z: ForexFactory carries 4.60% against 4.35%, NAB, CBA and Westpac all forecast it, ANZ forecasts it and a second hike in November to 4.85%, and pricing is 92-94%. Trimmed mean inflation is stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band, the Australian 10-year at 5.4120 is the highest of the majors, and CPI on Wednesday carries a 4.1% consensus against 3.5%. None of that has weakened. What has weakened is the thing underneath it, and it is new: September's Australian PMIs rolled over hard. Manufacturing fell to 49.3 from 52.0, into contraction; services to 51.4 from 53.2; composite to 50.8 from 52.7; consumer confidence to 84.4 from 88.9. Alongside that, copper - the cleanest AUD commodity proxy - fell 1.35% to 6.6052. And the tell is in the currency itself: AUD/USD is 0.70268, up 0.06%, which is nothing at all for a currency whose central bank hikes in under 24 hours. A fully priced hike arriving into deteriorating surveys and a soft commodity leg is a +2, not a +3, and the two-step sell-the-fact remains the specific risk: a cautious statement Tuesday, then a CPI print below 3.5% Wednesday. Sterling is the other side of the energy trade and it keeps +2 with a stronger case than yesterday. November 5 pricing has moved up to roughly 80-86% from about 75%, Goldman Sachs now explicitly forecasts the November hike, and the September vote was 6-3 with three members already voting for an immediate increase. Bailey's position is the most explicitly energy-conditioned on this board - high energy prices make it harder to leave rates on hold, and the longer the volatility persists the greater the probability of a hike - and Brent up 18.33% on the month is that condition intensifying rather than fading. UK CPI at 3.1% in August was the first print above 3% since March and the Bank forecasts a peak above 4% in early 2027. Bailey speaks Thursday at 08:00Z. The risk is fiscal rather than monetary: the gilt 10-year at 5.3890 is the second-highest yield of the majors and it is rising for the wrong reason, with the October 28 Budget on the same day as four central bank decisions. The euro holds +1 and picks up one genuinely new constraint. Euro-area inflation is 3.2% with core at 2.4%, the September flash on Friday at 09:00Z carries a 3.7% headline forecast with core at 2.5%, German preliminary CPI lands Wednesday at 0.5% m/m against 0.2%, and the PMIs improved to 53.1 composite and 53.0 services. Against that, negotiated wage growth has decelerated to 3.0% from 3.4% and consumer confidence slipped to -16.5. October 29 is priced near a coin flip at 53% for no change, and the new detail that matters is that October is a non-projection meeting - no updated staff forecasts accompany it - which historically lowers the odds of a move and makes Friday's flash the input that decides December instead. Lagarde speaks three times this week, today at 13:30Z. The dollar holds +2 and this is the week its thesis gets examined properly. The Fed is at 4.00%, October is about 70% priced, and the PMI complex is the strongest on the board at 58.4 composite, 58.7 services and 57.0 manufacturing. The September 16 SEP, verified on federalreserve.gov, has the funds rate at 4.1% for 2026 and 2027, 3.9% for 2028 and 3.2% in the longer run, with core PCE at 3.4% then 2.5% - one more hike, then a year of holding. But core PCE on Wednesday is forecast at 0.3% m/m from 0.2% while payrolls on Friday are forecast at 98K against 162K, and consumer confidence has already fallen to 48.1 from 51.7. Accelerating core inflation into decelerating hiring is the stagflationary combination that would take the 70% down, and rising crude is ambiguous for the dollar rather than supportive: it raises the inflation side and taxes the household side. The yen stays 0 and MIXED, and it is today's weakest major, with USD/JPY at 157.783 up 0.34%. The reason is mechanical - Japan is the purest energy importer here and Brent up 18.33% on the month is a straight terms-of-trade tax. The offset is real and getting closer: the BoJ hiked to 1.25% in September, the next meeting is October 28, former executive director Kazuo Momma put a consecutive-meeting hike at 20-30% while describing the base pace as once a quarter, and Tokyo core CPI on Thursday at 23:30Z is forecast at 2.4% against 1.8%, which is a large acceleration. Wages are running at 4.7%. So the yen is a carry funder with a hawkish tail, which is why the XXX/JPY longs here are carry positions at moderate conviction rather than a directional yen short, and why JPYBASKET is a RANGE. The July 31 joint intervention remains the reason to treat 160 as defended rather than as a target. New Zealand stays -1 and one number got settled: October 28 is 88% priced for no change at 2.75%, which resolves the contradictory pricing this page flagged yesterday in favour of the hold. Governor Breman has said elevated oil could push near-term inflation past the September forecast, and NZ inflation is 4.1%, but the offsetting data is the worst combination here - unemployment rising to 5.6% and wage growth of only 2.1%. NZD/USD at 0.56720 was actually the best major today at +0.18%, a bounce off a month down 4.11%; the relative case against seven banks that are hiking or being pushed to hike is what keeps it at -1. Metals and equities both flip, and both for the same reason. Gold and silver go SHORT from LONG: the haven bid was tested on the single best day it could have had and did not appear, while the US 10-year at 5.2090 and a real yield near 2.84% make the carry punitive. Silver is worse than gold because its industrial leg has copper falling 1.35% underneath it. EU50 flips from SHORT to LONG at low conviction, and the reason is precisely the leg that separates it from the DAX: banks are its heaviest sector and the Euro Stoxx Banks index rose 1.38% today, the strongest move on the page, because a Bund at 3.6210 and an ECB still 47% live for October are good for lenders. The offsetting leg is French political risk, with the OAT at 4.7260, the widest of the core - so banks dominate, but they do not make it a high-conviction long. GER40 goes to RANGE rather than long, because it does not have that bank weight and it does have the gas problem, with EU gas up 1.67% to 73.09. Copper is a RANGE: the physical squeeze is intact with the Yangshan premium at US$124 a tonne, up 72% in September and the highest in nearly four years, and LME available stock at 139,650 tonnes, but Shanghai inventories rose 2.4% to 56,073 tonnes after three weeks of decline and the dollar is firm. The cleanest trades follow directly from the regime call. The best tickets are the CHF crosses against the banks that are hiking on energy - USD/CHF long at high conviction on a 400bp policy gap, and GBP/CHF, EUR/CHF and AUD/CHF long on the same logic - because they need no view on whether the strait reopens, only on the fact that a 0.00% rate cannot answer an energy shock. AUD/NZD long at high conviction survives the AUD downgrade intact, because it is a three-point gap between a bank hiking tomorrow and a bank 88% priced to hold, and GBP/NZD long expresses the same thing with Bailey's condition attached. USOIL long stays, at medium conviction and sized for the specific risk that Trump expects talks to resume this week and the rejection was never formally delivered. What to be careful of: the honest weakness in today's page is that it is reading a regime off one session's price action, and the session in question is a Monday morning with the RBA, Australian CPI, US core PCE and payrolls all still ahead. If Thursday's Tokyo CPI and Friday's euro-area flash both print hot, the energy-inflation frame gets confirmed and the CHF shorts extend; if payrolls come in near 90K and the Fed's 70% starts to slip, the dollar leg of it is the first thing to go.

today.headline: The RBA hiked 25bp to 4.60% unanimously, in line with the 4.60% consensus, and dropped the conditional from its guidance - it now pledges to raise further 'if needed' rather than 'if upside risks materialise'
today.read: UP from +2 to +3, and the reason is the statement rather than the figure, which was never in doubt at 92-94% priced. TE confirms 4.60% from 4.35% against a 4.60% consensus, unanimous, the fourth increase of 2026 after February, March and May, and the highest Australian cash rate since 2011. Australia now carries the highest policy rate of these eight economies outright - 60bp above the Fed's upper bound, 85bp above Bank Rate, 210bp above the ECB deposit rate and 460bp above the SNB - so the carry that was being anticipated is now banked. The single most tradeable line is the guidance change. August committed the Board to raising further 'if upside risks materialise'; today it commits to raising further 'if needed', and the body explains why the condition was dropped: 'some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising'. Two August passages vanished with it - policy described as 'somewhat restrictive', and the line that inflation would not return to around the midpoint until late 2027 - replaced by the judgement that 'a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted'. This page named the bear case precisely yesterday: a statement that frames 4.60% as sufficient. It did the opposite. It also pre-empted tomorrow's print, saying 'recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected' and that higher fuel prices have partially passed through to other goods and services, and it named a new inflation source August did not carry - AI-related demand lifting global technology goods prices. The Board answered the survey problem too, which is what justifies the full notch back: June-quarter output was stronger than expected at the margin, labour eased 'broadly as expected' against August's 'a little more than expected', and leading indicators are 'broadly stable'. What it conceded is housing, and it broadened - prices now falling in 'most' capital cities against August's 'some', new housing loans declining noticeably, and a new line on uncertainty about the housing downturn's effects. Forward, the risks are ordered by clock. Bullock's press conference is within the hour and can undo the tone; monthly CPI lands tomorrow at 01:30Z with CPI y/y forecast 4.1% against 3.5%, and a print at or below 3.5% is still the cleanest sell-the-fact on this page. The tape is the caution: AUD/USD at 0.70263 is up only 0.12% on a delivered hike, and copper fell again to 6.5422, -3.21% on the week, so the commodity leg still is not confirming. Practical read: AUD/NZD and AUD/CHF longs stay HIGH on four- and five-point score gaps that are now delivered rather than expected; GBP/AUD flips from RANGE to SHORT because the timing difference the range was built on has resolved in Australia's favour; AUD/USD and AUD/CAD come off RANGE to LONG at low-medium, sized for tomorrow's CPI and for US core PCE and payrolls.

today.headline: The franc was given the cleanest possible haven test and failed it, with USD/CHF up 0.18% to 0.82972 on the day crude rose 2.64%
today.read: DOWN from 0 to -2, a two-notch move, and it needs the reason stated precisely because it reverses yesterday's call rather than adjusting it. Twenty-four hours ago CHF was upgraded from -1 to 0 on the argument that a war being re-escalated to a schedule is exactly when the franc bids. That argument was handed an ideal test - an escalation headline over a weekend, Brent opening up 2.64% at 107.074 - and the franc weakened instead, to 0.82972 against the dollar, up 1.04% on the week and 2.64% on the month. Gold falling 2.09% in the same session says the missing haven demand is a general feature of this regime rather than a franc quirk: expensive oil is being traded as an inflation event, and an inflation event rewards yield, which is the one thing the franc does not have. Take the haven leg out and what remains is verified from the SNB's September 24 assessment and is the weakest structural position on this board. The policy rate is 0.00% for a fifth consecutive meeting. The conditional inflation forecast is 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for both 2027 and 2028, which requires no move in either direction for two years. The Bank has returned to its standard wording that it will be active in the FX market as necessary, which in an appreciating-franc regime is a standing bid to sell. Schlegel has ruled out any appetite for negative rates by citing their undesirable side effects. The Swiss 10-year is 0.6490, a 456bp disadvantage to the US. Forward, the next inputs are Swiss CPI on Thursday at 06:30Z, forecast 0.0% m/m against 0.4%, and Schlegel speaking the same day at 15:30Z. Practical read: the CHF crosses are now the cleanest longs on the page - USD/CHF, EUR/CHF, GBP/CHF and AUD/CHF all at HIGH conviction - because they need no view on whether the strait reopens, only on the fact that 0.00% cannot answer an energy shock. What invalidates it is an actual attack that closes the strait harder rather than a negotiation that stalls.

today.headline: Bond markets now price a 68% chance of a Bank of Canada hike on October 28 against 32% for a hold, and that is new this week
today.read: UP from 0 to +1, and this is the largest genuinely new fact on today's page rather than a reinterpretation of an old one. Yesterday CAD was moved to 0 on the argument that a rising barrel restores Canada's terms of trade and brings Macklem's hawkish conditional back into reach. The pricing has now done that explicitly: 68% for a 25bp increase on October 28, against 32% for a hold, on a rate that has been frozen at 2.25% through seven consecutive decisions. Macklem supplied the logic himself at the September 2 meeting - the global energy shock remains the biggest tailwind to higher prices, and inflationary risks had become sharper since July with oil persistently high and no end in sight to the conflict, while the inflation risk from counter-tariffs is fairly modest. Brent at 107.074, up 6.71% on the week and 18.33% on the month, is that condition met, and for a net energy exporter it arrives as a terms-of-trade gain at the same time as an inflation input, so both halves push one way. The domestic picture has improved at the margin too: August retail sales rebounded 1.3% m/m after -0.7%, Q2 GDP came in at 0.8% q/q and 1.1% y/y from 0.1%, and core CPI is 2.4% with producer prices at 12.4%. What keeps CAD at +1 rather than higher is what the barrel cannot fix: August employment fell 41.7k after +75.1k, and services and composite PMIs at 46.8 and 47.8 remain the only contracting readings on this board. Forward, monthly GDP tomorrow at 12:30Z, forecast 0.1% against 0.3%, is the immediate test, then the Business Outlook Survey on October 19 and the Monetary Policy Report on October 28 where the oil assumption is the thing to read. Practical read: USD/CAD comes off LONG to RANGE, because a 175bp gap stops widening when the Fed is 70% priced and the BoC 68% for the same day and the barrel now works against the long; AUD/CAD drops to RANGE; CAD/JPY long at MED is the clean way to own the oil story inside FX; NZD/CAD short is the better way to be short a weak antipodean than to be short Canada.

today.headline: The yen is today's weakest major at 157.783, taxed by Brent up 18.33% on the month, while Tokyo CPI on Thursday is forecast to jump to 2.4% from 1.8%
today.read: UNCHANGED at 0 and MIXED, and the two sides are getting further apart rather than cancelling more quietly. Against the yen, the mechanism is arithmetic: Japan is the purest energy importer on this board, and a month in which Brent rose 18.33% is a straight transfer out of Japanese national income. That is why USD/JPY rose 0.34% to 157.783 today, the largest move in the majors, on a session when the dollar index barely moved at +0.08%. For the yen, the policy path is closing in. The BoJ raised to 1.25% in September, three months after June rather than the previous roughly six-month cadence, and the next meeting is October 28 - the same day as the Fed, the BoC and the RBNZ. Former BoJ executive director Kazuo Momma, who ran monetary policy, put the odds of a consecutive-meeting hike at 20-30% while describing the basic pace as quarterly, which makes October a live tail rather than the base case. The input that decides it lands Thursday at 23:30Z: Tokyo core CPI is forecast at 2.4% y/y against 1.8% previous, a large acceleration, with national wages already running at 4.7%. Forward, the constraint above spot is official rather than economic. The joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 is a matter of record and 160 has been the zone authorities defended, so the honest framing is a 157-160 range rather than a trend, and a sustained break through it needs either a dovish BoJ surprise or explicit official tolerance. Practical read: the XXX/JPY longs on this page - USD/JPY, EUR/JPY, GBP/JPY, AUD/JPY and CAD/JPY - are carry positions against a low-yielder rather than a directional short of the yen, which is why none of them is above MED conviction and why JPYBASKET is a RANGE rather than a short. A hot Tokyo print on Thursday is the event that would turn all of them.

today.headline: November 5 pricing moved up to roughly 80-86% from about 75% and Goldman Sachs now forecasts the hike, with Brent up 18.33% on the month feeding Bailey's condition
today.read: UNCHANGED at +2, but the case underneath it is materially firmer than yesterday and that matters for conviction rather than for the score. Three things have moved in sterling's favour. Pricing for November 5 has risen to roughly 80-86% from about 75% a week ago. Goldman Sachs has moved to an explicit call for the November hike. And the condition Bailey himself set is intensifying rather than fading: he has said that persistently high energy prices make it harder to leave rates on hold and that the longer the volatility persists, the greater the probability of an increase - with Brent at 107.074, up 6.71% on the week and 18.33% on the month, that is the condition tightening in real time. The starting point is already hawkish: September's decision held Bank Rate at 3.75% in a 6-3 vote, so three of nine members were voting for an immediate increase before any of this. UK CPI at 3.1% in August was the first print above 3% since March and a five-month high, energy-driven, and the Bank's own forecast has inflation peaking above 4% in early 2027. The counterweight is the labour market - wage growth cooled to 3.9% from 4.2%, the payrolled-employees series is still shrinking at -26.1k, and the composite PMI slipped to 51.7 from 52.5 - which is why this is +2 and not higher. Forward, Bailey speaks Thursday at 08:00Z and Ramsden today at 10:00Z. The risk is fiscal and it is concentrated on one date: the gilt 10-year at 5.3890 is the second-highest yield of the majors and is rising on borrowing rather than growth, and the Budget lands October 28, the same day as four central bank decisions. Practical read: GBP/CHF long at HIGH conviction is the cleanest expression, because it pairs the most energy-sensitive hawk with the only central bank that cannot respond; GBP/NZD long at HIGH pairs it against the one bank expected to sit still; GBP/USD stays RANGE with both currencies at +2 and the fiscal risk offsetting the monetary case.

today.headline: October 28 is 88% priced for no change at 2.75%, which settles yesterday's contradictory pricing in favour of the hold
today.read: UNCHANGED at -1, with one number resolved that this page flagged as uncertain yesterday. The file previously noted contradictory readings, including a 75% figure for a move to a 3% OCR on October 28; the verified pricing is 88% for no change at 2.75%, with the next increase sitting at the December 9 meeting. That settles the relative case, which is the whole of the bear argument: being the one central bank explicitly expected to sit still while six others are hiking or being pushed toward hiking by the same energy shock is what keeps NZD at the bottom of this board regardless of its own inflation rate. And its own inflation rate is high - 4.1% for the June quarter, tied for the highest here, driven largely by fuel and related prices from the conflict, with Governor Anna Breman having said elevated oil could push near-term inflation past the September projection and the Committee seeing upside risks to the central track. What lets the Committee look through that is the most conflicted domestic combination on this board: unemployment has risen to 5.6% from 5.4% while wage growth is only 2.1%, the lowest here, so there is no second-round mechanism for a fuel shock to work through. Q2 GDP did surprise up at 2.6% y/y and the composite PMI is 52.5, so this is relative rather than absolute weakness. Forward, there is no New Zealand red folder this week, which means NZD trades entirely as the funding leg of other people's central banks until the October 28 cluster. NZD/USD at 0.56720 was actually today's best major at +0.18%, a bounce off a month down 4.11%, and the NZ 10-year at 5.1400 is the lowest of the antipodeans. Practical read: AUD/NZD long and GBP/NZD long stay HIGH conviction, EUR/NZD long stays MED, NZD/USD short stays MED; NZD/JPY is the one to leave alone, a RANGE between two currencies whose carry and whose scores point opposite ways.

today.headline: EUR holds +1 with the inflation case firmer but October 29 now identified as a non-projection meeting, which is why the path moves from hike to hold
today.read: UNCHANGED at +1, with the score steady and the rate path revised for a structural reason rather than a data one. The inflation case has strengthened: euro-area headline is 3.2% with core at 2.4%, Friday's September flash at 09:00Z carries a 3.7% headline forecast with core at 2.5%, German preliminary CPI lands Wednesday at 06:29Z forecast 0.5% m/m against 0.2%, and growth has turned up with the composite PMI at 53.1 from 52.0 and services at 53.0 from 51.6. What changes the path is that October 29 is a non-projection meeting - no updated staff macroeconomic forecasts accompany the decision - which historically lowers the probability of a move and makes Friday's flash the input that decides December 17 instead of October. Reported pricing at 53% for no change is consistent with that. The offsetting domestic evidence is the wage track and the consumer: negotiated wage growth has decelerated to 3.0% from 3.4%, consumer confidence slipped to -16.5, and retail sales fell 0.6% m/m - an inflation impulse arriving through energy rather than through wages is the kind a central bank can wait out, which is exactly what a non-projection meeting lets it do. Forward, Lagarde speaks three times: today at 13:30Z, Tuesday at 11:00Z and Thursday at 13:30Z, with the monetary policy accounts on October 8. AUD.when: November 3 is live but is not yet the consensus base case. AUD.note: TE re-verified: the cash rate is 4.60 percent, raised 25bp today from 4.35% in a unanimous decision - the fourth increase of 2026 after February, March and May, and the highest Australian cash rate since 2011. This is now the highest policy rate of these eight economies, 60bp above the Fed's upper bound, 85bp above Bank Rate, 210bp above the ECB deposit rate and 460bp above the SNB. The tradeable content was always going to be the statement rather than the figure, and read against August the statement is hawkish in one specific and unambiguous way: the guidance conditional has been removed. August committed the Board to raising further 'if upside risks materialise'; today it commits to raising further 'if needed', because the body of the statement declares those risks are no longer hypothetical - 'some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising'. Two other August passages are simply gone: the characterisation of policy as 'somewhat restrictive', and the timing line that inflation was not expected to return to around the midpoint until late 2027. In their place: 'a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted'. The Board also pre-empted tomorrow's print, saying 'recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected' and that higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to other goods and services, and it named a new inflation source August did not carry - AI-related demand driving rapid growth in global technology goods prices. The dovish material in the statement is housing and it broadened: prices have now fallen in 'most' capital cities against August's 'some', new housing loans have declined noticeably, and the Board added uncertainty about the effects of the housing downturn to its risk list. But labour actually read less dovish than August - conditions eased 'broadly as expected' where August said 'a little more than expected', leading indicators are 'broadly stable', and June-quarter output was stronger than expected at the margin. The sequencing risk this page flagged has therefore half-resolved in the hawkish direction, and the other half lands in roughly 21 hours: monthly CPI tomorrow September 30 at 01:30Z, with CPI y/y forecast 4.1% against 3.5%, CPI m/m 0.5% against 1.0% and trimmed mean m/m 0.3% against 0.5%. Governor Bullock's press conference is the nearer risk and it can undo the statement's tone within the hour. The counterweights are unchanged by today: September manufacturing PMI at 49.3 from 52.0 is still in contraction, services 51.4 and composite 50.8, consumer confidence 84.4, and copper has kept sliding to 6.5422 USD/lb, -0.42% today and -3.21% on the week, so the commodity leg is still not confirming. NAB's framing is the honest medium-term caveat: further hikes support AUD near term, but Australia may finish tightening before its peers and be among the first forced to reverse. Australian 10-year 5.4120, the highest of the majors. AUD/USD 0.70263, +0.12% - a muted first reaction that says the figure was priced and the statement was the news.

That is precisely why the Committee can look through a 4.1% print, and why 88% of the market expects it to. The Bank expects inflation elevated this year, back inside the band by mid-2027 and at the 2% midpoint later next year. strength.forward: ⚖️ Range into October 29, and the rate path moves from hike to hold on a structural fact rather than a change of view. October 29 is a non-projection meeting: no updated staff macroeconomic forecasts accompany the decision. That matters because the euro-area inflation impulse is arriving through energy rather than through wages - negotiated pay has decelerated to 3.0% from 3.4% - and an energy impulse without a wage impulse is exactly the kind a central bank prefers to confirm before acting on. Without fresh projections to justify a move, the natural sequence is to let Friday's flash and the October data land, then decide at December 17 when the staff forecasts are updated. Reported pricing at 53% for no change fits that. The hawkish input is real and getting larger: a 3.7% headline flash against 3.2% released would be the highest euro-area print of this cycle's second leg, German preliminary CPI at 0.5% m/m is a big monthly step, and the growth data has turned up rather than down, which removes the excuse of a weakening economy. So what is expected is a hold on October 29 with hawkish language, and a December decision that Friday effectively sets up. Lagarde speaks three times this week - today at 13:30Z, Tuesday at 11:00Z, Thursday at 13:30Z - and those are the places the framing shifts. strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish into October 28, upgraded from a hold, and this is the largest genuinely new fact on today's page. The pricing is the evidence: 68% for a 25bp increase against 32% for a hold, on a rate frozen through seven consecutive decisions. It moved because the condition Macklem stated at the September meeting is being met in front of him - he named the global energy shock as the biggest tailwind to prices and said risks had sharpened since July with no end in sight to the conflict. Canada is the one economy here where a rising barrel pushes both the inflation input and the terms of trade the same way, so the energy-inflation regime is unambiguously CAD-positive rather than two-sided as it is for the dollar. What holds the score at +1 rather than higher is that the labour market and the surveys are genuinely bad and the barrel cannot reach them: employment fell 41.7k in August after +75.1k, and services and composite PMIs at 46.8 and 47.8 are the only contracting readings on this board. A central bank does not hike into contracting surveys unless inflation forces it, which makes this path more fragile than the Australian or British one. What is expected into the meeting is a live decision rather than a formality, with the Monetary Policy Report on the same day and the oil price assumption inside it the thing to read. The immediate test is monthly GDP tomorrow at 12:30Z, forecast 0.1% against 0.3%. What invalidates the upgrade is a GDP miss combined with Brent falling back under US$100, which would restore the domestic story over the commodity one and take the 68% down fast. The Business Outlook Survey on October 19 is the other checkpoint.

The reason it can is the labour market, and it is the specific asymmetry worth owning: 4.1% inflation with 2.1% wage growth and unemployment rising to 5.6% is a relative-price shock, not an inflation process, and a committee can look through it without losing credibility. What is expected into the meeting is therefore a hold with an acknowledgement of near-term upside risk, and the December decision left genuinely open. catalysts.event: RBA cash rate decision and rate statement - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: The event of the week. ForexFactory's red folders carry Cash Rate and RBA Rate Statement at 04:30Z with forecast 4.60% against 4.35% previous; NAB, CBA and Westpac all forecast the hike, ANZ forecasts it plus a second increase to 4.85% in November, and market pricing is 92-94%. The case: trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band with the decline stalled, headline 3.5%, Q2 GDP 2.1% y/y, August employment +39,493, and Governor Bullock telling a parliamentary committee that some of the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising, with global oil prices cited as a driver. Against it, and new this week: September PMIs deteriorated sharply, with manufacturing falling to 49.3 from 52.0 and into contraction, services to 51.4 from 53.2, composite to 50.8 from 52.7, and consumer confidence to 84.4 from 88.9. Because the hike is 92-94% priced, the tradeable content is entirely the statement - specifically whether 4.60% is framed as sufficient or as a step. RESULT: the Board hiked 25bp to 4.60%, in line, unanimously - the fourth increase of 2026 and the highest cash rate since 2011, taking Australia to the highest policy rate of these eight economies, 60bp above the Fed's upper bound and 210bp above the ECB deposit rate. The statement resolved hawkish on the one line that mattered: it pledges to raise further 'if needed', dropping August's 'if upside risks materialise', because 'some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising'. Gone with it are August's description of policy as 'somewhat restrictive' and its line that inflation would not reach around the midpoint until late 2027; in their place, 'a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted'. The Board pre-empted tomorrow's CPI by stating that growth and inflation have been higher than expected, and named AI-related demand lifting global technology goods prices as a new inflation source. Its concession was housing: prices now falling in 'most' capital cities against August's 'some', with new housing loans declining noticeably. AUD/USD 0.70263, +0.12%.

catalysts.event: Australia CPI y/y, CPI m/m and trimmed mean CPI m/m - ABS
catalysts.note: The most awkward sequencing on the page: this lands roughly 21 hours AFTER the RBA decides, so the Bank hikes into a print it has not seen. ForexFactory's red folders carry CPI y/y forecast 4.1% against 3.5% previous, CPI m/m 0.5% against 1.0%, and trimmed mean CPI m/m 0.3% against 0.5%. A 4.1% print would tie Australian headline inflation with New Zealand's as the highest of these eight economies, and would open the path to ANZ's forecast of 4.85% by year end. The asymmetry is what matters for AUD: a print at or above 4.1% validates Tuesday and extends the path, while anything at or below 3.5% turns a 92-94% priced hike into a policy error against September PMIs that have already rolled into contraction - the cleanest sell-the-fact setup on this page.

catalysts.event: US core PCE price index m/m and final GDP q/q - BEA
catalysts.note: ForexFactory red folders at 12:30Z: core PCE m/m forecast 0.3% against 0.2% previous, and final GDP q/q 1.5% unrevised. Core PCE is the Fed's own target measure and the September 16 SEP has it at 3.4% for 2026 falling to 2.5% in 2027, so an acceleration to 0.3% m/m is a direct challenge to the projection that underpins the one-more-hike-then-hold path. This is the first of the two prints that examine the roughly 70% pricing for October 28, and it is the hawkish one - the dovish one is payrolls two days later. The combination is what matters rather than either alone: accelerating core inflation with decelerating hiring, into a consumer confidence reading already down to 48.1 from 51.7, is a stagflationary mix that gives a data-dependent Fed room to wait even with inflation above target.

geopolitics: The market spent Monday telling us what Saturday actually meant, and it disagreed with the obvious reading. Take the sequence. Through the previous week Iran had submitted a seven-day roadmap through Qatari mediation: the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions affecting Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire covering the wider region including Lebanon, and in return Iran reopens the Strait of Hormuz at the end of seven days and restarts talks on its nuclear programme. Araghchi's own framing was conditional - if certain conditions are met, the strait opens on day seven and talks restart the same day. On Saturday Trump rejected it publicly, said Tehran had overplayed its hand, and the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterms. Yesterday this page read that as the death of the de-escalation trade and repriced six currencies on it. Monday priced something narrower and more precise. Crude rallied exactly as a re-escalation would imply - Brent +2.64% to 107.074, WTI +1.85% to 94.119, up 18.33% and 9.75% respectively on the month - but every asset that should have moved with it on a war premium went the other way: gold -2.09% to 4195.62, silver -3.50% to 62.009, the franc weaker with USD/CHF at 0.82972, and European equities higher with the DAX +0.30%, the Euro Stoxx 50 +0.38% and the Euro Stoxx Banks index +1.38%. The reconciliation is in the detail of what was said rather than in the headline. Trump also said he expects negotiations to resume this week. Araghchi confirmed that the rejection had still not been communicated to Iran officially through mediators, said Iran is waiting for a definitive US response, and claimed the US ambassador has not read the proposal - while keeping diplomacy explicitly on the table even as he said Iran is prepared to resume fighting, including to a doomsday war. Iran has not withdrawn or softened its conditions. So the channel is open, the rejection is rhetorical rather than procedural, and what the market priced is a delayed reopening rather than a collapsed negotiation. That distinction is the whole transmission mechanism for FX this week, and it runs through central banks rather than through risk appetite. A strait that stays shut for longer means a sustained energy price rather than a spiking one, and a sustained energy price is an inflation problem that policy has to answer. So the barrel now sets the reaction function of six of these eight central banks, and it is doing so in the same direction: Bailey has said explicitly that the longer high energy prices persist the harder it is to hold, and November 5 is 80-86% priced; Macklem named the global energy shock as the biggest tailwind to prices and October 28 is now 68% priced after seven holds; Bullock said the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising with oil cited as the driver, and the RBA hikes tomorrow; euro-area energy pass-through is carrying the headline toward a 3.7% flash on Friday; Breman has warned elevated oil could push New Zealand inflation past the September projection; and Japan simply pays the bill as the purest importer here. The two that do not fit are instructive. The dollar is genuinely two-sided, because higher crude raises the inflation side that argues for October while taxing a consumer already at 48.1 confidence. And the franc has no reaction function at all: at 0.00% with a conditional forecast of 0.7% then 0.8% then 0.8%, the SNB cannot answer an energy shock, which is why the one currency that should have gained from escalation is the one this page now scores at -2. The practical consequence is that the haven trades are the wrong expression of this conflict and the carry trades are the right one. Long USOIL is the direct ticket. Long the CHF crosses against the banks the barrel is pushing to hike is the indirect one, and it is cleaner, because it pays whether the strait reopens in a week or a quarter - it only stops paying if oil collapses far enough to remove the inflation problem entirely. The asymmetry to respect is that the same open channel that makes this a delay rather than a war can close it in the other direction too: Qatar is still mediating, Araghchi is still waiting on official channels, and the June 17 memorandum showed how abruptly the process can reopen.
